definition: A machine learning approach that combines predictions from multiple models to produce a more accurate and robust result than any single model.
details: Ensemble methods (including bagging, boosting, and stacking) exploit the fact that different models often make different errors, so combining them can cancel out individual weaknesses.

explainer.lead: Ensemble learning asks several models for a prediction, then combines their answers. It matters because models often make different mistakes, so a well-combined group can be more accurate and robust than any one member.

tiers.eli5: Imagine asking three friends whether it will rain: one looks at the clouds, one checks the wind, and one remembers yesterday’s weather. If you combine their answers instead of trusting just one friend, a single bad guess is less likely to ruin the result. Ensemble learning does this with computer models.
tiers.practitioner: Train several models and combine their outputs, commonly by averaging numeric predictions or taking a majority vote for classes. Bagging, boosting, and stacking are standard ensemble approaches. The main pitfall is a group whose members make the same errors, since combining them provides little correction.
tiers.paperLevel: Given base predictors f_1(x), ..., f_M(x), an ensemble computes y_hat = Combine(f_1(x), ..., f_M(x)), for example by averaging or majority voting. Its benefit depends on individual errors differing enough for aggregation to cancel some of them; highly correlated errors limit that benefit.

explainer.example: Three classifiers examine the same email and predict “spam,” “not spam,” and “spam.” A majority vote produces the ensemble’s final prediction: “spam.”

usedIn.name: Classification
usedIn.detail: Multiple class labels can be combined, for example by majority vote.

usedIn.name: Regression
usedIn.detail: Numeric predictions from several models can be combined, for example by averaging.

explainer.intuition: A single model can fail in its own particular way, but different models often fail on different cases. Combining their predictions can reduce the influence of those individual weaknesses.
howItWorks: Train multiple models to solve the same prediction task.
Give each model the same new input.
Collect their predictions, which may disagree.
Combine the predictions into one final answer, such as by averaging or voting.
explainer.whyItMatters: Ensembles provide a practical way to improve accuracy and robustness without relying on one model to handle every case well. Their strength comes from complementing individual models rather than merely repeating them.
misconceptions: More models do not automatically help if they all make the same mistakes.
An ensemble is not a single prediction copied several times; it combines outputs from multiple models.

diagram.caption: Several models predict independently, and a combiner turns their outputs into one result.
